text:
**Keep the Joined Line: The Case for Teaching Cursive in Primary School**

Every few years, a familiar argument returns. Children type on tablets from the age of four. Adults rarely write more than a shopping list or a signature. Surely, the reasoning goes, the hours spent teaching seven-year-olds to loop an "l" and link it to an "e" could be better used on coding, or on typing. Joined-up handwriting is a Victorian relic, and primary schools should let it go.

I think this is wrong. Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting, and should teach it better than many do now. My case rests on three claims. Joined writing is a more efficient physical skill than the alternatives. It supports thinking and learning in ways keyboards do not fully replicate. And the "relic" argument misunderstands what schools are for.

**Handwriting is not going away**

Start with the premise that nobody writes by hand any more. It is only half true. Adults write less by hand than they once did, but children do not. Pupils still sit exams with a pen. They take notes in lessons, fill in worksheets, label diagrams, sketch out maths, and write cards and letters. In most countries, high-stakes written examinations remain handwritten. A child who cannot write quickly and legibly by hand is at a daily, concrete disadvantage, whatever the world of work looks like in twenty years.

The question, then, is not whether children should write by hand, but how. The realistic options are print only, a mix, or a joined style taught deliberately. And here the case for joining is strongest.

**Why joining helps**

Printed letters require the pen to lift after every character. Each lift is a small interruption: the hand stops, repositions, restarts. Joined writing keeps the pen moving. Letters flow into one another, and whole words become single motor patterns rather than strings of separate decisions. With practice, this makes writing faster and less tiring, which matters when a fifteen-year-old has ninety minutes to write three essays.

Speed is not the only advantage. Teachers who work with struggling writers often point out that a consistent joined style can reduce the common reversals and spacing errors that print invites. When every letter is formed with the same entry and exit stroke, there is less ambiguity about where one word ends and the next begins, and letters such as "b" and "d" are harder to confuse because they are formed differently from the first stroke. The evidence here is mixed and I will not overstate it. But the practical experience of many classroom teachers, and of occupational therapists who work with children with motor difficulties, is that a flowing, rhythmic script can be easier for some pupils than the stop-start of print.

There is also a point about fluency and cognitive load. Writing is hard because it asks a child to do two things at once: decide what to say, and physically produce it. If the second task consumes too much attention, the first suffers. This is well established in research on writing: children whose handwriting is not automatic tend to write shorter, simpler texts, because their working memory is occupied by letter formation. Automaticity is the goal, and automaticity comes from practice with a consistent, efficient movement. A joined script, taught early and practised regularly, is one of the best routes to it.

**The thinking hand**

The second claim is subtler. A growing body of research suggests that writing by hand engages the brain differently from typing. Studies using brain imaging and learning tasks have found that forming letters by hand can strengthen letter recognition in young children, and that note-taking by hand can encourage students to process and summarise rather than transcribe verbatim. Not every finding has replicated cleanly, and researchers disagree about how large these effects are. I do not want to claim that cursive makes children cleverer. That would be the kind of overreach that gives the pro-handwriting side a bad name.

What I will claim is more modest. Handwriting slows a child down just enough to think. A keyboard lets you produce text faster than you can form ideas, and for a young writer that is not always a virtue. The physical act of shaping words creates a rhythm of composition that many writers, including many adult professionals, still prefer for first drafts. Teaching children a comfortable, fluent handwriting gives them access to that mode of thought. Denying them it, in the belief that keyboards make it redundant, closes a door before they know what is behind it.

Handwriting also carries fine-motor development. Learning to control a pen through continuous, patterned strokes is good training for the small muscles and the hand-eye coordination that children use in everything from drawing to using tools. Of course, children can develop these skills in other ways. But writing is a purposeful, curriculum-relevant way of doing so, and a joined script, with its repeated curves and links, is particularly good practice.

**The objections**

The first objection is time. The school day is crowded, and every minute on handwriting is a minute not spent on reading, maths or computing. This is a fair point, and it is why I would not defend the long, joyless handwriting drills of the past. But the time required is modest. Short, frequent, well-taught sessions, ten or fifteen minutes a few times a week in the early years, are enough for most children to become fluent. The cost is small, and the benefit lasts for a lifetime of use.

The second objection is typing. Children need keyboard skills, and they do. I am not arguing against teaching typing; I am arguing against treating it as a replacement. Both skills matter, they serve different purposes, and a curriculum that can teach children to read, count and swim can teach them to type and to write by hand. The choice is a false one.

The third objection is that cursive is hard to read, and that print is clearer. This confuses good joined writing with bad. Badly taught, hurried cursive can be an illegible scrawl. But so can print. The answer is better teaching: a simple, consistent model, introduced early, with attention to letter shapes and spacing. Many schools now use a simple "print-script with exit strokes" approach, in which children learn print letters with small joining flicks and gradually link them. That is a sensible compromise, and it still counts as teaching joined-up writing.

The fourth objection is that cursive is merely traditional. But tradition is not an argument against something, any more than it is an argument for it. The test is whether the skill is useful. Fluent handwriting is useful. Joined writing is the most efficient way of achieving it that we have found.

**What schools are for**

There is a deeper issue beneath the practical ones. Primary education is not only preparation for the labour market of 2040, which no one can predict. It is also the transmission of a shared culture, and the building of basic human capacities. Being able to read a handwritten letter from a grandparent, to sign your name, to write a note to a neighbour or a line in a birthday card, are small but real parts of being a literate person. A child who cannot read cursive cannot read the handwritten documents of the past, from family letters to historical archives, without help. A child who cannot write it has a thinner, more mechanical relationship with their own handwriting, which is among the most personal things a person makes.

None of this requires nostalgia. It requires only a recognition that the skills we teach young children should be judged by what they enable, and that the ability to write fluently, legibly and without effort by hand enables a great deal.

**A better way forward**

The right answer to the handwriting debate is not to abandon joined writing, but to reform how it is taught. Schools should adopt a simple, clear model and use it consistently across the school. They should introduce joining early, once letter formation is secure, rather than leaving it to Year 4 as an anxious afterthought. They should give left-handed children and those with motor difficulties specific support rather than a one-size-fits-all approach. And they should assess handwriting by fluency and legibility, not by how closely it matches a copybook.

Above all, they should be honest with children about why it matters. Not because "that's how it has always been done," but because writing by hand is a skill that makes everything else in school easier, and that will stay useful long after the next generation of devices has come and gone.

The keyboard is a wonderful tool, and children should learn to use it well. But the pen is a different tool, with different strengths, and a child who can use both has more options than one who can use only one. Joined-up handwriting deserves its place in the primary classroom: a small, efficient, humane skill, quietly doing its work.
